essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how to develop the pattern for a square-to-round transition piece by triangulation, including the true length diagram.
essays.modelAnswer: I draw the plan, showing the square end and the round end on the same centre, and the elevation, showing the height between them. I divide the circle in the plan into 12 equal parts and number the points. I join each corner of the square to the three or four circle points nearest it, which divides the surface into triangles at the corners and flat triangles on each side. The plan lengths of these lines are not true lengths, because the lines slope. I make a true length diagram: a vertical line equal to the height, with each plan length set out along the base; the line from the end of each plan length to the top of the height is the true length. I start the pattern at the seam, on the centre line of one flat side. I build the triangles one by one in order, using the true lengths for the sloping lines, the true length of the square's side, and the chord between circle points for the round edge. I join the round-edge points with a smooth curve, add any seam allowance, and check the pattern with a card model.
markingPoints: Draws plan and elevation; divides the circle into equal parts
Joins corners to circle points to form triangles
Builds a true length diagram from plan lengths and height
Starts at the seam and builds the triangles in order with true lengths and chords
Draws a smooth curve, adds allowances and checks with a model

essays.stem: Describe how to develop the patterns for a tee made of two pipes of the same diameter meeting at 90°, using the parallel line method.
essays.modelAnswer: I draw the front view of the main pipe and the branch, and an end view of the branch as a circle. I divide the branch circle into 12 equal parts and project these points along the branch as generator lines. Because the pipes are the same diameter, I can find where each generator meets the main pipe from the end view of the main pipe; in the front view the line of intersection appears as two straight lines meeting in a V. For the branch pattern, I draw a stretch-out line equal to the branch's mean circumference, divide it into the same 12 parts and draw a vertical line at each point. I carry the length of each generator from the front view to its matching line, then join the tops with a smooth curve, starting the seam on the shortest line. For the hole in the main pipe, I draw part of the main pipe's stretch-out, set out the distances round the main pipe to each point from the end view, carry the positions along from the front view, and join them to form the hole shape. Finally I check both patterns with a paper model.
markingPoints: Draws front and end views; divides the branch circle into equal parts
Finds the line of intersection (a V in the front view for equal pipes)
Branch pattern: stretch-out, matching lines, lengths carried across, smooth curve
Hole pattern on the main pipe developed from the main pipe's stretch-out
Places the seam sensibly and checks with a model

essays.stem: Explain how to set out a 90° lobster-back bend made of four pieces (three welded joints) in pipe, including the angles and how you would make and use a template.
essays.modelAnswer: A 90° bend with three joints turns 90 ÷ 3 = 30° at each joint, so each joint face is cut at half of that, 15°, from square on each pipe piece. The two end pieces have one square end and one end cut at 15°. The two middle pieces have both ends cut at 15°, so they are short on the throat (inside) and long on the back (outside). I work out the lengths from the bend radius: on the centre line, each middle piece is 2 × R × tan 15° long, and each end piece is R × tan 15° plus any straight length needed. I draw the pipe in elevation, divide its end view into 12 parts, and develop a wrap-around template for a 15° cut using the parallel line method. I make the template from thin sheet, mark the centre lines and the throat and back. I wrap it round the pipe, line up its marks with lines scribed along the pipe, scribe the cut, and cut and bevel. I check each piece's angle and length, tack the pieces with the centre lines lined up, and check the bend is 90° and in one plane.
markingPoints: Each joint turns 30°; each cut is 15° from square
Describes end pieces and middle pieces correctly
Works out piece lengths from the bend radius (R × tan 15° per half-piece)
Develops and marks a wrap-around template with centre lines
Cuts, checks, tacks in line and checks the 90° and the plane

essays.stem: Explain how plate thickness affects pattern development for cylinders, cones and bent parts, and give a worked example.
essays.modelAnswer: When plate is rolled or bent, the outside stretches and the inside is squeezed. Somewhere in between is a line that keeps its length, the neutral axis. For rolled plate, it is taken at mid-thickness, so patterns for cylinders and cones are developed from the mean sizes. For example, a cylinder 600 mm outside diameter in 10 mm plate has a mean diameter of 600 − 10 = 590 mm, so the plate length is 3.142 × 590 = about 1854 mm. Using the outside diameter would give 1885 mm, about 31 mm too long. For a cone, the mean diameters and mean slant height are used. For tight bends in sheet, the neutral axis lies nearer the inside, and the developed length is found from a bend allowance chart or the maker's figures. Thick plate also needs weld preparation, so the pattern edges may need bevels, and the root gap must be allowed for in the length. On thin sheet the effect is small, but on thick plate it can decide whether the part fits.
markingPoints: Explains stretching, squeezing and the neutral axis
Rolled plate: develop from mean sizes
Correct worked example (mean diameter and plate length)
Bends in sheet: bend allowance from charts or the maker
Allows for weld preparation and root gap on thick plate

essays.stem: A conical hopper is a frustum with a top diameter of 800 mm, a bottom diameter of 300 mm and a vertical height of 500 mm (mean sizes). Work out the slant heights and the sector angle for its pattern, showing your working.
essays.modelAnswer: The radii are 400 mm at the top and 150 mm at the bottom, a difference of 250 mm over a height of 500 mm. By similar triangles, the full cone's apex is 400 × 500 ÷ 250 = 800 mm below the top, which is 300 mm below the bottom. The slant height of the full cone, used as the large radius of the pattern, is √(800² + 400²) = √800 000 = about 894.4 mm. The slant height of the small cone cut off, used as the small radius, is √(300² + 150²) = √112 500 = about 335.4 mm. The slant height of the hopper side is 894.4 − 335.4 = 559.0 mm, which checks with √(500² + 250²) = 559.0 mm. The sector angle is 360 × base radius ÷ slant height = 360 × 400 ÷ 894.4 = about 161°. Checking with the small end, 360 × 150 ÷ 335.4 also gives about 161°. To set out the pattern, I draw two arcs of 894.4 mm and 335.4 mm from one centre, with a sector of 161°, and add the seam allowance.
markingPoints: Uses similar triangles to find the apex (800 mm from the top)
Large slant height about 894.4 mm
Small slant height about 335.4 mm, with a check of the side length
Sector angle about 161° (360 × r ÷ L)
Explains how the pattern is set out, with allowance

essays.stem: Explain how to construct an ellipse by the concentric circles method, and give two places where a fabricator might need an ellipse.
essays.modelAnswer: I draw the major (long) axis and the minor (short) axis at 90° to each other, crossing at the centre. From the centre, I draw two circles: one with a diameter equal to the major axis and one equal to the minor axis. I divide the large circle into 12 equal parts by drawing lines through the centre, which also cut the small circle. From each point on the large circle, I draw a line parallel to the minor axis, and from the matching point on the small circle, I draw a line parallel to the major axis. Where each pair of lines crosses is a point on the ellipse. I join all the points with a smooth curve, using a flexible curve or by careful freehand, and check that it is the same in each quarter. A fabricator needs an ellipse to mark the hole where a round pipe passes through a sloping plate or roof at an angle, for an oval duct or tank end, and for the shape of a round pipe cut at an angle.
markingPoints: Draws the major and minor axes at 90°
Draws two concentric circles from the axes
Divides the circles and draws lines parallel to each axis
Crossing points joined with a smooth curve and checked
Gives two correct uses (angled pipe hole, oval duct, angled pipe cut)

essays.stem: Explain why and how large patterns are split into segments and nested on standard plate sizes to save material. Give an example.
essays.modelAnswer: Plate comes in standard sizes, such as 1220 mm × 2440 mm or larger sheets the supplier stocks. A large pattern, such as the side of a big cone or hopper, may not fit on one plate, or may leave a lot of waste when it does. Splitting the pattern into two or more segments lets each piece fit on a plate, and lets pieces be turned and fitted close together, which is called nesting. For example, a cone pattern with a sector of 240° may be split into two 120° segments, which can be laid head to tail on one sheet with much less waste. Seams are placed where they are easy to weld and inspect and where they are not in the most stressed part. Each extra seam adds welding, so the team weighs the plate saved against the welding cost. Every segment must have its seam allowance and edge preparation, and be marked with match marks so that the pieces go together in the right order. The nesting plan is drawn first, to scale or in CAD, and checked before any plate is cut.
markingPoints: Explains standard plate sizes and why large patterns may not fit
Explains splitting into segments and nesting to reduce waste
Gives a sensible example
Balances plate saved against extra welding; places seams sensibly
Adds allowances and match marks, and checks the nesting plan first

essays.stem: Describe how you would check a fabricated transition piece or hopper against the drawing before it is welded into place, and what you would record.
essays.modelAnswer: I first check the drawing revision and the key sizes I need: the sizes of each end, the height, the offset if any, and the positions of the seams and flanges. I check the square or rectangular end by measuring each side and both diagonals, which should be equal, so I know it is square and not twisted. I check the round end by measuring the diameter at several angles and the girth with a tape against the calculated figure, to show it is round and the right size. I measure the height between the two ends at several points to check that they are parallel and the right distance apart, and check the centre lines line up. I check the seams for gaps and alignment, and that the edges are prepared for welding. If it must fit other parts, I offer it up or check the bolt holes against the mating flanges. I record each measurement, the drawing sizes, the tolerance, whether it passes, the date and my name on an inspection sheet, and report anything outside tolerance before welding.
markingPoints: Checks the drawing revision and key sizes first
Square end: sides and equal diagonals
Round end: diameter at several angles and girth against calculation
Height, parallel ends, centre lines, seams and fit with mating parts
Records results against tolerances, signs and reports any faults

essays.stem: As team leader, explain how you would organise your team to develop, mark, cut, form and check a cone frustum, with roles and checks at each stage.
essays.modelAnswer: I brief the team with the drawing and agree the plan. One member works out the slant heights and sector angle and a second member checks the sums independently. Two members draw the pattern full size on thin sheet or card, add the seam allowance and match marks, and make a quick paper model to prove it; I check the model's sizes before we move on. One member then transfers the pattern to the plate, using the centre and arcs and marking the seam and match marks, while another checks the marking. The cutting is done by the trained members with the right tools, and the edges are deburred and prepared. For forming, two members work the rolls under my supervision, checking the curve with a sweep template as they go. Finally, all members check the frustum: both diameters, the girths, the height and the seam gap, and one records the results on the inspection sheet. At each stage the work stops if a check fails, and we find and fix the cause before carrying on.
markingPoints: Briefs the team and gives clear roles
Independent check of the calculation
Full-size pattern with allowances and a model, checked
Marking, cutting and rolling with checks during the work
Final inspection recorded; work stops to fix any failed check

essays.stem: Compare the parallel line, radial line and triangulation methods of development: the shapes each suits, how each works, and their limits.
essays.modelAnswer: The parallel line method is used for shapes whose surface lines run parallel, such as cylinders, pipes, prisms and ducts, including those cut at an angle and pipe intersections. The shape is divided by parallel lines, the stretch-out is drawn equal to the girth, and the length of each line is carried across from the elevation. It cannot be used for tapering shapes. The radial line method is used for shapes whose surface lines all meet at one point, such as right cones, pyramids and their frustums. The pattern is drawn from the apex with the true slant length as the radius, and the base length stepped round the arc. It needs the apex to be found, which is hard when the cone is very flat, and it does not work for oblique cones. Triangulation is used for any shape that the other two cannot handle, such as transition pieces, oblique cones and offset hoppers. The surface is split into triangles, the true length of each line is found, and the triangles are built up in order. It works for almost any shape, but takes longer and small errors can add up.
markingPoints: Parallel line: cylinders, prisms, pipe cuts; stretch-out and carried lengths
Radial line: right cones and pyramids, from the apex with true slant lengths
Triangulation: transitions, oblique cones; triangles with true lengths
States a limit of each method
Makes a clear comparison

practical1.title: Develop, make and inspect a square-to-round transition piece in sheet steel
practical1.brief: As a team, develop and make a square-to-round transition piece from 1 mm or 1.2 mm mild steel sheet to the sizes the assessor gives you (for example a 300 mm square end, a 200 mm diameter round end, both on the same centre, 200 mm apart). First, plan the job: the method, the seam position, the allowances and who does what. Draw the plan and elevation full size, divide the round end into 12 parts, build the true length diagram and develop the full pattern by triangulation, with a seam allowance. Make a paper or card model and check it before marking the steel. Transfer the pattern to the sheet, cut it with snips or a nibbler, deburr, and form the piece over a bench stake or by hand, then join the seam by tack welding, spot welding or riveting as the assessor directs. Inspect the finished piece: sides and diagonals of the square end, diameter and girth of the round end, and the height, and record the results. Each member does at least one stage while the assessor watches, and checks a stage done by another member. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the piece and the inspection sheet are finished and the area is clean.
materials: 1 mm or 1.2 mm mild steel sheet, about 1000 mm × 600 mm
Paper or card for the drawing and model
Steel rule, tape, square, compass or dividers, trammels, scriber, protractor
Snips or nibbler, files or deburring tool, bench stakes and mallet
Means of joining the seam (tack welder, spot welder or rivets), clamps
Calculator, plan sheet and inspection sheet
photos: The plan, elevation and true length diagram
The full pattern on paper, with the seam allowance
The pattern transferred to the steel sheet
The formed transition piece with its seam joined
Members measuring the square end diagonals and the round end, with the inspection sheet
checklist: Helped plan the job and can explain why triangulation is used
Built true lengths correctly from plan lengths and the height
Developed the pattern accurately, with the seam allowance
Checked the model before marking the steel
Marked, cut and deburred the sheet accurately and safely
Formed the piece to shape, with ends square and round as drawn
Measured and recorded the finished sizes against the drawing
Checked another member's stage and left the area clean
safety: Wear gloves when handling and cutting sheet; deburr all edges
Wear safety glasses when cutting and forming
If welding the seam, follow the Centre's hot work rules, with screens, PPE and ventilation
Keep the floor clear of offcuts and sheet; work on benches where you can
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Develop wrap-around templates and fabricate an equal tee and a three-piece 90° lobster-back bend in steel pipe
practical2.brief: As a team, develop, make and tack up two pipe fittings from steel pipe the assessor gives you (for example 100 mm or 4 inch nominal bore). First, plan the work: the calculations, who does what, and the checks. For the equal tee, develop the branch pattern and the hole pattern in the main pipe by the parallel line method. For the 90° lobster-back bend with three pieces (two joints), work out the cut angle (22.5° from square) and the length of each piece from the bend radius the assessor gives. Draw each development full size and make wrap-around templates in thin sheet or card, with centre lines and quarter marks. Scribe lines along the pipes, wrap the templates, mark and cut the pipes, and grind the cut edges clean. Tack the tee and the bend together with their centre lines in line. Check the tee for 90° and fit, and the bend for 90°, its radius and being flat (in one plane), and record the results. Each member makes or uses at least one template and cuts at least one piece while the assessor watches. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the fittings and the inspection sheet are finished and the area is clean.
materials: Steel pipe, about 1.5 m, of the size the assessor gives
Thin sheet or card for the templates; drawing paper
Tape, steel rule, square, protractor, compass, scriber, soapstone or paint marker
A straight length of angle to scribe lines along the pipe
Angle grinder with cutting and grinding discs, or a pipe cutter; files
Welding set for tacking, clamps or a pipe vice; inspection sheet
photos: The calculations and the full-size developments
The wrap-around templates with centre lines and quarter marks
A template wrapped on the pipe and the cut line marked
The cut pieces of the bend and the tee, before tacking
The tacked tee and lobster-back bend
Members checking the bend for 90° and flatness, with the inspection sheet
checklist: Took part in the calculations and got the cut angle and lengths right
Developed an accurate template with centre lines and quarter marks
Lined up the template with the lines on the pipe and marked accurately
Cut and cleaned the pipe safely, with the work held firmly
Tacked the pieces with the centre lines in line
Checked the fittings for angle, fit and flatness and recorded the results
Worked as a team and left the area clean
safety: Clamp the pipe in a pipe vice or on a stand before cutting; never hold it by hand
Wear a face shield, safety glasses, hearing protection and gloves when grinding
Follow the Centre's hot work rules when tacking: screens, PPE, ventilation and an extinguisher
Treat cut and tacked pipe as hot and sharp; deburr edges
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
